title: The Particle は (wa)
subtitle: Topic marker
reading: わたし は がくせい です。
explanation: は marks the topic of the sentence. It tells the listener 'as for X...' — what follows is a comment about X. Despite being written with the hiragana character 'ha', it is always pronounced 'wa' when used as a particle.

examples.reading: これ は ほん です。
きょう は いい てんき です。
わたし は すし が すき です。
examples.romaji: watashi wa sushi ga suki desu.

tips: は is the most common particle in Japanese — look for it early when parsing a sentence.
The topic is often 'known information' — both speaker and listener are aware of it.
は can be omitted in casual speech once the topic is established.

title: The Particle が (ga)
subtitle: Subject marker
reading: ねこ が ねている。
explanation: が marks the grammatical subject — the thing performing the action or being described. Unlike は (which marks known topics), が introduces new or emphasized information. Think of it as answering 'what' or 'who' is doing something.

examples.reading: だれ が きました か？
あめ が ふっています。
すし が おいしい です。

tips: は vs が: は introduces a known topic; が introduces new or focused information.
が is used with question words like 誰 (だれ, who) and 何 (なに, what).
With adjectives expressing preference (好き, 嫌い), が marks the thing liked/disliked.

title: です and ます — Polite Form
subtitle: Polite sentence endings
reading: わたし は すし を たべます。
explanation: です (desu) is the polite copula — roughly equivalent to 'is/am/are'. ます (masu) is the polite verb ending. Both make sentences formal and are used with strangers, elders, and in business. Drop them for casual speech with friends.

examples.jp: 毎日日本語を勉強します。
examples.reading: まいにち にほんご を べんきょう します。
すし を たべません。

tips: ません (masen) is the negative of ます — 'I don't do X'.
でした (deshita) is the past of です — 'was/were'.
Polite form is always safe — when in doubt, use it.

title: The Particle を (wo)
subtitle: Direct object marker
reading: みず を のみます。
explanation: を marks the direct object of a verb — the thing receiving the action. It's pronounced 'o' even though it's written with the character 'wo'. Only transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) use を.

examples.reading: ほん を よみます。
にほんご を べんきょう します。
ちゃ を のみましょう。

tips: を is always pronounced 'o', never 'wo'.
を only appears before verbs — never at the end of a sentence.
Some verbs like する (suru, to do) and なる (naru, to become) don't take を.

title: The Particle に (ni)
subtitle: Destination, time, and indirect object
reading: がっこう に いきます。
explanation: に is a versatile particle. It marks: (1) destination of movement ('to'), (2) specific points in time ('at'), (3) the indirect object ('to/for'), and (4) location of existence (with ある/いる). Context determines which meaning applies.

examples.reading: さんじ に あいましょう。
とうきょう に すんでいます。

examples.jp: 先生に花をあげました。
examples.reading: せんせい に はな を あげました。
examples.en: I gave flowers to the teacher.

tips: に for time: only specific times (3:00, Monday) — not relative time like 'today' or 'tomorrow'.
に vs へ: both can mean 'to', but に implies arrival while へ emphasizes direction.
に with ある/いる: marks where something exists.

title: Essential Greetings
subtitle: First words for every situation
explanation: Japanese greetings change with the time of day and social context. Using the right greeting shows cultural awareness and respect. Here are the essential ones you'll hear throughout the valley.
tips: おはよう is casual, おはようございます is polite — use the polite form with strangers.
こんにちは is used from late morning until evening.
さようなら is formal — またね is the casual 'see you' for friends.

title: Shopping Phrases
subtitle: Buying and bargaining at shops
reading: いくら です か？
explanation: When shopping at the market or a shop, these phrases will help you ask about prices, request items, and complete purchases politely. The shopkeepers in the valley will appreciate your effort!

examples.reading: これ を ください。
いくら です か？

examples.jp: もう少し安くなりませんか？
examples.reading: もう すこし やすく なりません か？
examples.en: Could it be a little cheaper?

tips: ください (kudasai) is the magic word — 'please give me X'.
高い (takai) means both 'expensive' and 'high/tall' — context tells you which.
Bargaining is uncommon in regular shops but fine at markets and festivals.

title: Dining Phrases
subtitle: Eating out with confidence
explanation: Japanese dining etiquette includes specific phrases before and after meals. いただきます expresses gratitude for the food and those who prepared it. ごちそうさまでした thanks the host or cook after finishing.

examples.reading: ごちそうさま でした。
メニュー を ください。
おかいけい を ください。

tips: Say いただきます before eating, not after ordering.
ごちそうさま (casual) or ごちそうさまでした (polite) after finishing.
Slurping noodles is acceptable and shows enjoyment!

title: The Art of Bowing (お辞儀)
subtitle: More than just a greeting
explanation: Bowing is central to Japanese communication. It conveys greeting, gratitude, apology, and respect. The depth and duration of a bow carry meaning: a slight nod for casual greetings, 15° for customers, 30° for formal situations, and 45° for deep apologies.

examples.jp: よろしくお願いします。
examples.reading: よろしく おねがい します。
examples.en: Please treat me well (said with a bow).

examples.jp: ありがとうございます。
examples.reading: ありがとう ございます。
examples.en: Thank you very much (said with a bow).
Excuse me / I'm sorry (said with a bow).

tips: A slight nod (会釈, eshaku) ~15° is fine for everyday greetings.
The deepest bow (最敬礼, saikeirei) ~45° is for apologies or profound gratitude.
Foreigners aren't expected to bow perfectly — effort is appreciated.

title: おもてなし — Japanese Hospitality
subtitle: The spirit of selfless service
explanation: おもてなし is the Japanese philosophy of hospitality — anticipating needs before they're expressed and providing service from the heart without expectation of return. You'll see it in shops, restaurants, and inns throughout the valley.

examples.jp: どうぞお座りください。
examples.reading: どうぞ おすわり ください。
おまたせ しました。

tips: Shop staff say いらっしゃいませ when you enter — a simple nod is a fine response.
おもてなし means the staff anticipates your needs — don't be surprised by attentive service.
Tipping is not customary in Japan — good service is included.

title: Nature Words in the Valley
subtitle: Words you'll see on signs and shrines
explanation: As you explore the valley and beyond, you'll encounter nature words on signposts and shrines. These words appear frequently in place names and directions. Learning them will help you navigate the world.
tips: Many place names combine these: 山 (yama) + something = 'Mt. Something'.
森 (mori) means a large forest; 林 (hayashi) is a smaller woods.
Look for these kanji on signposts throughout the world!

title: Direction Words — Finding Your Way
subtitle: Compass directions for navigation
explanation: Direction words appear on every signpost in the world. The cardinal directions are also used in place names — knowing them helps you read maps and understand where NPCs are directing you.
tips: Mnemonic: 北 (kita) has the same first sound as 'kita' in 'kita e' (to the north).
東 (higashi) has 日 (sun/day) + 木 (tree) — 'sun rising from behind trees' = east.
Look for these on the colored signposts at road junctions!

title: い-adjectives and な-adjectives
subtitle: Two types of adjectives
reading: たかい やま、しずか な もり
explanation: Japanese has two types of adjectives. い-adjectives end in い and conjugate on their own (高い→高くない). な-adjectives need な before a noun (静かな森). Some look like い-adjectives but are actually な-adjectives — memorize each one.

examples.reading: しずか な もり
きれい な はな

tips: い-adjectives: 高い (takai), 大きい (ookii), 小さい (chiisai), 美味しい (oishii).
な-adjectives: 静か (shizuka), きれい (kirei), 元気 (genki), 有名 (yuumei).
きれい ends in い but is a な-adjective — watch out for exceptions!

title: て-form of Verbs
subtitle: The Swiss Army verb form
explanation: The て-form is a verb form used for requests, connecting sentences, and many grammatical patterns. To make it: る-verbs drop る and add て (食べる→食べて). う-verbs change the ending (書く→書いて). This form is essential for everyday conversation.

examples.reading: かいて、よんで、はなして。

tips: て + ください = polite request: 'please do X'.
て-form alone (casual) = 'do X' — a direct but friendly command.
て-form connects verbs: 'I did A and B and C'.

title: Reading Valley Signs
subtitle: Practice reading real signposts
reading: すしだに へ ようこそ
explanation: Signs throughout the valley use basic kanji and kana. Practice reading them! Each sign you encounter in the world teaches a real word. Try to read the Japanese first, then check the reading and meaning.
tips: 入口 and 出口 are everywhere — learn them first!
注意 (chuii) appears on warning signs — slow down when you see it.
Many signs use kanji you'll learn from shrines and books in the world.

title: 四季 — The Four Seasons
subtitle: Seasons shape Japanese life
explanation: Japan's four distinct seasons influence food, festivals, clothing, and speech. Each season has associated words and customs. The game's seasonal system (Bloomtide, Builder's Muster, Champion's Week) mirrors this cultural rhythm.
tips: 桜 (sakura) viewing in spring is a national tradition called 花見 (hanami).
紅葉 (momiji) viewing in autumn is called 紅葉狩り (momijigari).
Seasonal words appear in the game's seasonal events — look for them!

title: Emergency & Help Phrases
subtitle: When you need assistance
reading: たすけて ください！
explanation: These phrases could be important in real travel situations. In the game, you'll hear them from NPCs in trouble. Learn them for both game quests and real-world travel safety.

examples.reading: たすけて ください！
びょういん は どこ です か？

examples.jp: 警察を呼んでください。
examples.reading: けいさつ を よんで ください。
みち に まよいました。

tips: すみません (sumimasen) also means 'excuse me' — use it to get attention.
道に迷いました is useful when exploring — NPCs may give you directions!
In the game, NPCs in trouble use these phrases — recognizing them starts quests.
